title: Build cache size limit on Vercel increased to 5 GB
description: The build cache size limit on all Vercel build machines has been increased to 5 GB. This allows projects to save more installed dependencies and framework files for reuse between deployments, which can reduce install and build times. Build machines are the compute environments that install dependencies and build your project before deployment. Previously, caches were discarded if they exceeded 1.5 GB on Basic and Standard, 3 GB on Enhanced, or 4.75 GB on Turbo, leaving the next build without a cache. The change applies automatically across all build machine types at no additional charge, with no configuration required. Learn more in the build cache documentation . Read more

title: Parallel Decisions now available on AI Gateway for free
description: Parallel Decisions Fast from Parallel is now available on AI Gateway and is free through November 23, 2026. It searches the live web to answer typed questions about companies, products, policies, and other changing information, returning probabilities and cited evidence for your application to act on. Use it to enrich CRM records, check eligibility, route leads, or verify claims against current sources. Boolean questions return the probability of yes, Choice questions select from options you define, and Score questions assess an ordered rubric. Related questions share context and retrieved evidence in one request. Use parallel/parallel-decisions-fast as the model name. No separate Parallel account is required. These examples ask the same web-grounded question through the AI SDK, TypeSafe-compatible API, and OpenAI-compatible Decisions API. Citations include source URLs, optional titles, and evidence excerpts. They apply to the whole request, rather than mapping individual sources to each answer. Your application can use answer probabilities to act automatically above a threshold and send uncertain results for review. AI Gateway tracks these requests in logs and spend budgets alongside other model requests. Read the decision model documentation for question types, or browse the model catalog . Read more

title: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
description: When we first launched Workflow SDK, the goal was simple: write regular async JavaScript, and let the SDK keep it running through crashes, deployments, and long waits. Last year, we shipped just that , with the world-class developer experience Vercel is known for. Then we watched what our customers built with it. More than 4 billion steps and 700 million runs later, two clear patterns have emerged. The first is automation : Traditional workflows that move data, process orders, coordinate background jobs, manage subscriptions, and run ETL and data pipelines. The second is agents and harnesses : Agents are expensive and long running, so they naturally require durability too. As those workloads matured, Workflow matured with them. Our priorities have always been security, reliability, and performance. Here’s how Workflow SDK 5 delivers on all three. More secure workflows The Workflow event log stores step arguments and return values so a run can recover after a crash or deployment. That data can include sensitive customer information, model context, credentials, and tool-call results. Persisting it requires strong protection. Workflow SDK encrypts every payload end to end , before it leaves your code. Workflow and step inputs and outputs, hook payloads, and stream data are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a unique key for each run. With encryption enabled, any Workflow SDK backend, including Vercel, only sees and stores ciphertext. Plaintext is decrypted in your deployment or in authorized observability tools. Encryption with zero configuration on Vercel On Vercel, encryption needs no setup and no code changes. Each run’s key is derived from a key scoped to the deployment that created it, so a run can only decrypt its own data. Your workflow code doesn’t change: Because Vercel manages the keys by default, observability keeps working. Names, timings, and statuses are always visible, and when you need to see a payload, you can decrypt it in the dashboard or the CLI. Decryption happens in your browser or terminal, follows the same permissions as the project’s environment variables, and every request is recorded in your team’s audit log. Encryption on self-hosted Worlds Encryption is implemented in the SDK, so it can also protect payloads on self-hosted Worlds before they reach storage, queues, or streams. A custom World enables encryption by implementing getEncryptionKeyForRun() with your key management . Return the same 32-byte key for each run on every call so the SDK can encrypt new payloads and decrypt them during replay: More security work in v5 Cross-run writes are sealed too. When code resumes another run’s hook, starts a run in another deployment, or writes into a stream forwarded from another run, the payload is encrypted to the target run’s public key. The writer can encrypt for that run without reading its existing payloads. You can also limit how long sensitive data is stored. With payload retention set to experimental_retention: 0 , inputs, outputs, and stream contents are deleted as soon as a run completes or fails. The run’s metadata stays visible in observability. A redesigned trace viewer The redesigned trace viewer makes runs easier to navigate, with span search, zoom, a minimap, and local inspection during development. Run attributes are new in v5. They let you attach searchable context to a run, such as an order ID, and then find runs by it. Attributes are plaintext, so they should not contain secrets. Workflows in every region In Workflow SDK 4, every run lived in iad1 . Even when a project was deployed to several regions, each run’s event log, queue, and streams were only stored in one region, so a step running anywhere else made cross-region requests to record its progress. For v5, we deployed Workflow infrastructure to every Vercel Function region . Each run has its own home region: its state, queue dispatch, and streams are served from the region where it started, without cross-region round trips on the hot path. By default, a run starts in the region of the function that starts it. Deploy to several regions, and each run stays close to the user who triggered it, with no configuration: To place a run somewhere else, pass a region to start() . That lets a workflow run next to the database it reads and writes, or keep a customer’s data in the region where it has to stay: The region option decides where a run’s data lives. Your steps run where your app is deployed, so deploy to that region too if you want them to execute there. Existing v4 runs stay in iad1 . Infrastructure reliability Regional isolation also improves reliability. A disruption in one region does not have to stop new runs in healthy regions. For projects with Vercel Function failover configured, steps can execute in a fallback region while continuing to use the run’s original home region for state. That state remains pinned to its home region; it does not migrate during failover. With the help of anonymized telemetry and close collaboration with many customers, we found and fixed dozens of rare bugs and race conditions in the Workflow runtime. Workflow SDK also recovers on its own from more kinds of intermittent network errors. As a result, with Workflow SDK 5, we’ve seen almost no runs fail or stall because of a platform or runtime bug. Agent-ready performance In Workflow SDK 4, every step invocation involved a queue hop to start the step and another to continue the workflow. That is acceptable for slow background automations, but adds latency to the AI workloads developers are building today. Agent loops and harnesses can contain thousands of sequential events, high-throughput token streams, tool chains, and dynamic subagents. At that scale, the networking and CPU work around every step became a limit. In Workflow SDK 5, we rewrote large parts of the engine to minimize extra queue hops, unnecessary networking, and CPU work. Across the measured workloads, we saw 1.6× to 25× improvements in measured latency and overhead, while preserving the same developer experience and introducing no major breaking changes. The benchmarks below compare v5.2.0 with v4.8.12 on Vercel. Pick a measurement to see how v5 compares with v4, then play or scrub through the explainer to see exactly what each benchmark measures. Workflow SDK 5 includes hundreds of performance improvements to achieve this. Here are some of the major changes behind these numbers: Fewer queue hops In v4, each step handed execution back through the queue. In v5, an invocation can execute several steps inline, including parallel steps, before yielding for a wait, a hook, or an approaching timeout. The runtime also avoids unnecessary persistence round trips and folds step creation into execution. Fewer queue and network requests mean less CPU work and lower runtime overhead. In a five-step benchmark, p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 618 ms to 109 ms . Incremental replay Over a 1,020-step benchmark, v4’s p75 overhead grew with the event log : replaying the full event history took time proportional to its size. In the final sampled range, overhead reached 1,748 ms. On v5.2.0, it was 70 ms . The median time to finish all 1,020 steps fell from 21.0 minutes to 3.0 minutes. WebSocket streaming Durability should not make a streamed response fall behind its producer. On the Vercel World, v5.2.0 writes streams over WebSockets by default . In a benchmark replaying a 52.4-second agent response, median delivery dropped from 226.1 seconds to 53.5 seconds . Payload compression reduces the data stored and transferred. AI token streams average around 80% smaller after compression. These measurements describe one workload, in one region, against the Vercel World. They are a useful view of runtime overhead, rather than a prediction for every application. Benchmark results and methodology Measured October 8, 2026, on Vercel production in iad1 , against the managed Vercel World . Each version uses a separate deployment of the same app. Steps take 1 KB of JSON in and out. Selected results · v4.8.12 compared with v5.2.0 Measurement v4.8.12 v5.2.0 Change First step, p75 418 ms 172 ms 2.4× faster Between steps, p75 618 ms 109 ms 5.7× faster Late-run overhead, p75 1,748 ms 70 ms 25× lower 1,020 steps, median 21.0 min 3.0 min 7× faster Resume, p75 699 ms 425 ms 1.6× faster Stream delivery, median 226.1 s 53.5 s 4.2× faster Chunk trip time, p75 172 ms 102 ms 1.7× faster Runs with a chunk delayed >1 s 6 / 10 0 / 10 100% fewer The full results, including tails, are in the performance documentation . Worlds: the shared durability primitive Workflow SDK’s durable functions sit on a World : the interface for storing progress, dispatching work, and delivering streams. That same foundation also now supports fx and durable-harness , which adds durability to existing agent harnesses. Improvements to the shared storage, queue, and streaming infrastructure can benefit any consumer of a World. Optimizations inside the Workflow replay runtime apply to Workflow SDK; they do not automatically apply to every harness. Choose the integration around how you want to build: Workflow SDK : write durable application logic with use workflow and use step . WorkflowAgent : use @ai-sdk/workflow for an AI SDK agent loop inside a workflow. fx : embed and extend a native coding agent with libfx. durable-harness : keep an existing supported harness and add durability beneath it. Supports Pi and OpenCode , with experimental integrations for Claude Code and Codex in Vercel Sandbox. eve : build agents with durable sessions powered natively by Workflow SDK and Worlds. We’ll soon be adding more offerings to our catalog of SDKs and frameworks backed by Worlds for durability. Build with Workflow SDK 5 Besides the improvements above, Workflow SDK 5 also adds: In-flight cancellation with AbortController Searchable run attributes More framework integrations And more The v5 upgrade docs cover what changed. To start building a new workflow, install the SDK: Workflow SDK also has a Python SDK , now in beta, with the same durable workflows, steps, sleeps, and hooks. Read more

title: Vercel Sandbox now supports managed npm credentials
description: Vercel Sandbox can now install your team's private npm packages using credentials stored in team Shared Environment Variables . Custom registries such as GitHub Packages and JFrog Artifactory are also supported. Pass credentials: { npm: true } when creating a sandbox to let it use your team's existing npm credentials. Tokens stay outside the sandbox. The firewall adds authentication to install requests sent to your configured registries, so a coding agent can install dependencies without seeing the tokens. Update your Sandbox SDK or CLI to the latest version. Read the npm credentials documentation to get started. Read more

title: Python 3.15 now available as a Vercel Managed Image
description: Python 3.15 is now available as a Vercel Managed Image for Vercel Sandbox . To run a sandbox with Python 3.15, select vercel/sandbox/python:3.15 using the image option in either SDK or the --image flag in the CLI. The default universal image ( vercel/sandbox/universal:latest ) still ships Python 3.14 and is scheduled to switch to Python 3.15 on December 16, 2026. Learn more in the Vercel Sandbox images documentation . Read more

title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen now available on AI Gateway
description: Gemini 4 Hydrogen from Google is now available on AI Gateway. Gemini 4 Hydrogen succeeds Gemini 3.8 Flash, improving agentic coding, knowledge work, and tool use while staying in the same latency class. It handles longer engineering tasks and produces better-researched documents, spreadsheets, and presentations in fewer agent steps. Hydrogen follows system instructions, formatting requirements, and task boundaries more closely, with more reliable tool orchestration across long conversations. Improvements in visual reasoning and technical problem-solving support multimodal workflows, while stronger grounding reduces unsupported claims in search-backed answers and invented tool or test results in coding reports. Use google/gemini-4-hydrogen as the model name: To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup: Then select google/gemini-4-hydrogen in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details. Try Gemini 4 Hydrogen in the model playground . AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting , Zero Data Retention support , budgets for API keys , routing rules , and more. AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests. You can view all language models available on AI Gateway. Read more
